questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A displacement-time graph is shown for a particular wave.

A second wave of similar type has twice the intensity and half the frequency.

When drawn on the same axes, which graph would the second wave look like?
questions.stemText: A displacement-time graph is shown for a particular wave. A second wave of similar type has twice the intensity and half the frequency. When drawn on the same axes, which graph would the second wave look like? A  B  C  D

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Two simultaneous changes (amplitude via intensity ∝ A², and period) must be read off grids.
questions.misconception: Thinking amplitude is proportional to intensity rather than its square root

explanation.body:
Intensity $\propto$ amplitude$^2$, so twice the intensity means the amplitude is $\sqrt{2}$ times larger.

Half the frequency means the period is doubled, so the graph shows half as many cycles.

perOption.A: Doubles the amplitude, as if intensity were proportional to amplitude.
perOption.B: Correct. Amplitude $\times\sqrt{2}$ and period doubled.
perOption.C: Doubles the amplitude and doubles the frequency instead of halving it.
perOption.D: Correct amplitude, but the frequency is doubled instead of halved.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Unpolarised light of intensity $I_o$ is incident on a polariser. The transmitted light is then incident on a second polariser whose transmission axis is at 60° to the first. What is the intensity, in terms of $I_o$, of the light transmitted through the second polariser? A $\frac{1}{8}I_o$ B $\frac{1}{4}I_o$ C $\frac{3}{8}I_o$ D $\frac{1}{2}I_o$

stemImage.alt: Question 13: Unpolarised light of intensity Io is incident on a polariser. The transmitted light is then incident on a second polariser whose transmission axis is at 60° to

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Standard two-polariser Malus' law calculation.
questions.misconception: Forgetting that the first polariser halves unpolarised light, or using cos instead of cos²

explanation.body:
The first polariser transmits half of the unpolarised light: $\tfrac{1}{2}I_0$.

By Malus' law, $I = \left(\tfrac{1}{2}I_0\right)\cos^2 60^\circ = \tfrac{1}{8}I_0$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Applies $\cos^2 60^\circ$ but forgets the first polariser halves unpolarised light.
perOption.C: Uses $\sin^2 60^\circ$ instead of $\cos^2 60^\circ$.
perOption.D: Ignores the effect of the second polariser.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The compressions and rarefactions of a sound wave travelling in air in the positive x-direction are shown below.

Which statement is true about the diagram?
questions.stemText: The compressions and rarefactions of a sound wave travelling in air in the positive x-direction are shown below. P Q x Which statement is true about the diagram? A At P, the air pressure is minimum. B At Q, it is a position of antinode. C At Q, the air molecule is momentarily at rest. D At P, the air molecule is moving in the positive x-direction.

options.label: A
options.text: At P, the air pressure is minimum.

options.label: B
options.text: At Q, it is a position of antinode.

options.label: C
options.text: At Q, the air molecule is momentarily at rest.

options.label: D
options.text: At P, the air molecule is moving in the positive x-direction.

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires linking compressions/rarefactions in a progressive longitudinal wave to pressure and particle velocity.
questions.misconception: Applying standing-wave terms (nodes, antinodes) to a progressive wave; thinking molecules at a rarefaction are at rest

explanation.body: At P, the displacement curve crosses zero with a negative slope. As the curve shifts right, the displacement at P becomes positive, so the particle is moving in the positive $x$-direction.

perOption.A: P is at a compression, where the pressure is maximum.
perOption.B: This is a progressive wave, so it has no stationary-wave antinodes.
perOption.C: At Q, the particle passes through equilibrium in a rarefaction at maximum speed.
perOption.D: Correct. The particle at P moves in the positive $x$-direction.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A light source radiates light in all directions.

A small surface is placed at position S a distance 1.5 m from the light source. The plane of the surface is perpendicular to the direction of incidence of the light from the light source. The surface receives 1.4 W of power from the light of the source.

The power of the light source is now doubled and the surface is moved to position R a distance 3.0 m from the light source. The plane of the surface is still maintained perpendicularly to the direction of incidence of the light from the light source.

What is the power received by the surface at position R?
questions.stemText: A light source radiates light in all directions. A small surface is placed at position S a distance 1.5 m from the light source. The plane of the surface is perpendicular to the direction of incidence of the light from the light source. The surface receives 1.4 W of power from the light of the source. light source S R 1.5 m 3.0 m The power of the light source is now doubled and the surface is moved to position R a distance 3.0 m from the light source. The plane of the surface is still maintained perpendicularly to the direction of incidence of the light from the light source. What is the power received by the surface at position R? A 0.35 W B 0.70 W C 1.4 W D 2.8 W

appearances.originalFile: CJC PHY/H2/J2.H2.PRELIM.2026.Paper 1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Combines intensity proportional to source power and inverse-square distance.
questions.misconception: Applying only one of the two changes, or using 1/r instead of 1/r²

explanation.body: At distance $r$ from the source, the intensity is $I=P_s/(4\pi r^2)$. The surface receives $P=IA$, so for fixed area $P\propto P_s/r^2$. Doubling both $P_s$ and $r$ gives $P_R/P_S=2/2^2=1/2$, so $P_R=0.70\ \mathrm W$.

perOption.A: Applies the inverse-square decrease but misses the doubling of source power.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses an inverse-distance law, making the two doublings cancel.
perOption.D: Doubles the received power without accounting for the greater distance.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Three polarisers W, X and Y. Unpolarised light of intensity $I_0$ is incident normally on W, passes through X and emerges from Y. The axis of polarisation of each is shown by a dashed line. [Diagram: three discs; W axis at $30^\circ$ to the vertical, X axis at $40^\circ$ to the vertical, Y axis at $60^\circ$ to the vertical, all measured clockwise from vertical.] What is the intensity of the light that emerges from Y? A $0.11I_0$ B $0.32I_0$ C $0.43I_0$ D $0.64I_0$

stemImage.alt: Question 11: The diagram below shows three polarisers W, X and Y. 0I is incident normally onto the surface of polariser A beam of unpolarised light of intensity W, which the

appearances.originalFile: DHS Physics Prelim 2026/H2/DHS 2026 Y6 Physics H2 P1 Prelim (for external sharing).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Must halve for unpolarised light, then apply Malus' law twice using angle differences between successive axes.
questions.misconception: Using the absolute axis angles instead of the angle between successive polariser axes

explanation.body: The angles between successive polariser axes are $40^\circ-30^\circ=10^\circ$ and $60^\circ-40^\circ=20^\circ$. W transmits half the incident unpolarised intensity, so $I_W=0.5I_0$. By Malus's law, $I_X=0.5I_0\cos^2 10^\circ=0.4849I_0$, then $I_Y=I_X\cos^2 20^\circ\approx 0.428I_0\approx 0.43I_0$.

perOption.A: Uses the absolute $60^\circ$ angle at Y instead of its $20^\circ$ angle relative to X.
perOption.B: Uses the absolute axis angles instead of the angles between successive axes.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Exceeds the $0.5I_0$ already transmitted by W.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A light wave of amplitude $A$ is incident normally on a surface of area $S$. The intensity reaching the surface is $I$. The amplitude is increased to $2A$. The light is then focused onto a smaller area $\tfrac{1}{3}S$. What is the intensity on this smaller area? A $6I$ B $12I$ C $18I$ D $24I$

stemImage.alt: Question 12: A light wave of amplitude A is incident normally on a surface of area S. The intensity reaching the surface is I. The amplitude of the light wave is increased t

appearances.originalFile: DHS Physics Prelim 2026/H2/DHS 2026 Y6 Physics H2 P1 Prelim (for external sharing).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Two proportional reasoning steps: intensity proportional to amplitude squared, then power conserved over a smaller area.
questions.misconception: Treating intensity as proportional to amplitude rather than amplitude squared

explanation.body: At the original area, intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude, so doubling the amplitude gives $k(2A)^2=4I$. Focusing the same power onto one-third of the original area then gives $(4IS)/(S/3)=12I$.

perOption.A: Treats intensity as proportional to amplitude instead of amplitude squared.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Overestimates the gain from doubling the amplitude, which is a factor of four.
perOption.D: Doubles the result again even though squaring the amplitude ratio already accounts for the doubling.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The intensity of an unpolarised light decreases by 87.5% after passing through two polarisers.

What is the angle between the transmission axes of the two polarisers?
questions.stemText: The intensity of an unpolarised light decreases by 87.5% after passing through two polarisers. What is the angle between the transmission axes of the two polarisers? A 30° B 40° C 60° D 75°

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Malus' law with the halving at the first polariser and a percentage decrease to interpret.
questions.misconception: Forgetting the first polariser halves unpolarised light, or using cos instead of cos²

explanation.body: The first polariser reduces the incident intensity $I$ to $I/2$. The final intensity is $0.125I$, so Malus’s law gives $(I/2)\cos^2\theta=0.125I$. Hence $\theta=60^\circ$.

perOption.A: Using $30^\circ$ as the angle between the axes gives a transmitted fraction of $0.375$.
perOption.B: Using $40^\circ$ gives a transmitted fraction of about $0.293$, which is too high.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Using $75^\circ$ gives a transmitted fraction of about $0.033$, which is too low.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Two sheets of polaroid P and Q are placed such that their planes of polarisation are parallel as shown. A beam of unpolarised light passes through them and is incident on the detector. The intensity detected is $I$. [Diagram: incident unpolarised beam passes through polaroids P then Q (parallel vertical transmission axes), emergent beam goes to a detector] Which of the following is a possible angle through which Q can be rotated such that the intensity detected is reduced by 30%? A 213° B 226° C 237° D 253°

stemImage.alt: Question 16: Two sheets of polaroid P and Q are placed such that their planes of polarisation are parallel as shown. A beam of unpolarised light passes through them and is i

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Malus' law with an inverse cosine and the extra step of finding an equivalent angle beyond 180°.
questions.misconception: Interpreting 'reduced by 30%' as 'reduced to 30%'

explanation.body: By Malus’ law, the intensity after rotating Q through $\theta$ is $I\cos^2\theta$. A 30% reduction gives $0.70I=I\cos^2\theta$, with an acute solution of $33^\circ$. Since $\cos^2\theta$ repeats every $180^\circ$, $180^\circ+33^\circ=213^\circ$ is a possible rotation.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Its equivalent angle of $46^\circ$ transmits about 48% of $I$.
perOption.C: Its equivalent angle of $57^\circ$ transmits about 30% of $I$, a reduction of about 70%.
perOption.D: Its equivalent angle of $73^\circ$ transmits only about 9% of $I$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The diagram shows a graph of displacement against time for a sound wave.

The intensity of the sound is halved.

Which graph shows the new displacement of this sound wave?
questions.stemText: The diagram shows a graph of displacement against time for a sound wave. The intensity of the sound is halved. Which graph shows the new displacement of this sound wave? A  B  C  D

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs $I \propto A^2$ and reading amplitudes off grids while noticing frequency is unchanged.
questions.misconception: Thinking amplitude halves when intensity halves, or that frequency changes with intensity

explanation.body: Sound intensity $I$ is proportional to the square of the amplitude $A$. With $y$ as one vertical grid unit, the original amplitude is $4y$, so $\frac{I_{\mathrm{new}}}{I_{\mathrm{old}}}=0.50=\left(\frac{A_{\mathrm{new}}}{4y}\right)^2$. This gives $A_{\mathrm{new}}=2.8y$, with the original period unchanged.

perOption.A: Keeps the original amplitude and halves the period.
perOption.B: Keeps the original amplitude and shortens the period.
perOption.C: Halves the amplitude, which would reduce the intensity to one-quarter.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: The graph shows part of a transverse wave travelling along a string from left to right at time $t = 0$. [Graph: displacement $y$ against distance along string; P at a crest (amplitude $A$), S at zero displacement on a rising section, three-quarters of a wavelength to the right of P] The angular frequency of both particles P and S is $\omega$. The displacements of P and S are $y_P$ and $y_S$ respectively. Which of the following gives the correct relation between the displacement and time for either P or S and the phase difference between the motion of S and P? A $y_S = -A\sin\omega t$, $\tfrac{3}{4}\pi$ B $y_P = A\sin\omega t$, $\tfrac{3}{4}\pi$ C $y_P = A\cos\omega t$, $\tfrac{3}{2}\pi$ D $y_S = -A\cos\omega t$, $\tfrac{1}{2}\pi$

stemImage.alt: Question 13: The graph shows part of a transverse wave travelling along a string from left to right at time t = 0. displacement y P A • S distance along string • 0 The angul

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs particle direction from the wave's travel direction plus phase difference from the separation in wavelengths.
questions.misconception: Getting the direction of particle motion wrong for a travelling wave

explanation.body: P starts at its positive maximum, so its displacement is $y_P=A\cos(\omega t)$. S is $0.75\lambda$ to the right of P, so it lags by $2\pi(0.75)=3\pi/2$.

perOption.A: Uses the correct initial motion for S but gives half the phase lag.
perOption.B: Makes P start at zero displacement and gives half the phase lag.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Makes S start at $-A$ although it starts at zero.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Waves from a point source pass through an area that is $2.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ wide, as shown. [Diagram: rays diverging from a point source through a square of width $2.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ and further on through a square of width $16\ \mathrm{cm}$] Within this area, the intensity of the waves is $I$ and their amplitude is $A$. The waves reach a second area of width $16\ \mathrm{cm}$. What will be the intensity and amplitude of the waves when they reach the second area? A $I/8$, $A/4$ B $I/64$, $A/4$ C $I/64$, $A/8$ D $I/256$, $A/16$

stemImage.alt: Question 14: Waves from a point source pass through an area that is 2.0 cm wide, as shown. 16 cm 2.0 cm point source of waves Within this area, the intensity of the waves is

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Uses width ratio for distance, then inverse-square intensity and amplitude ∝ √I.
questions.misconception: Thinking amplitude falls in the same proportion as intensity

explanation.body: The cross-sectional area grows by a factor of $(16/2.0)^2=64$. The same wave power crosses both areas, so the intensity falls to $I/64$. Since intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, the amplitude falls to $A/\sqrt{64}=A/8$.

perOption.A: Scales intensity by the width ratio and gives an amplitude inconsistent with that intensity.
perOption.B: Gets the intensity right but takes the wrong square root for the amplitude ratio.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses $16$ as the width ratio instead of dividing by the initial width of $2.0\ \mathrm{cm}$.

questions.stemText: A longitudinal sound wave travels from left to right through air. The diagram below shows the equilibrium positions and the actual positions of a series of air particles through which the sound wave is passing. [Diagram: a row of 20 particles, each with a dashed vertical line marking its equilibrium position. Particles bunch together (compression) around B and around the right end, and spread apart (rarefaction) around C. A is displaced furthest to the right of its equilibrium line; B is displaced to the left; C sits on its equilibrium line; D is displaced to the right of its equilibrium line in the region between the rarefaction at C and the compression at the right.] Which of the particles has an acceleration that is opposite in direction to its velocity at this instant? A, B, C, D (labelled particles)

stemImage.alt: Question 14: A longitudinal sound wave travels from left to right through air. The diagram below shows the equilibrium positions and the actual positions of a series of air

appearances.originalFile: NYJC/H2/2026 NYJC H2 Phy 9478 P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires reading displacements off a longitudinal-particle diagram and deducing particle velocity from wave direction.
questions.misconception: Confusing compression/rarefaction position with direction of particle motion

explanation.body: Sketch particle displacement against equilibrium position. For a wave travelling to the right, the particle velocity has the opposite sign to the local slope of that graph. Particle D is moving away from equilibrium, while its acceleration points back towards equilibrium.

perOption.A: A is at an extreme displacement, where its instantaneous velocity is zero.
perOption.B: B is moving towards equilibrium, so its velocity and acceleration point in the same direction.
perOption.C: C is at equilibrium, where its speed is greatest and its acceleration is zero.
perOption.D: Correct. D moves away from equilibrium while accelerating towards it.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The diagram shows the positions $x$ of the particles along a progressive longitudinal wave at an instant in time. The wave travels at a speed of $16\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

[Diagram: a row of particles above an $x$ / m scale from 0 to about 32 m. The particles are bunched together (compressions) around $x \approx 8$ m and $x \approx 24$ m and spread out (rarefactions) around $x \approx 0$ m and $x \approx 16$ m.]

Which of the following statements is correct?

A The wavelength of the wave is 8.0 m.
B The particles are all in phase with one another.
C The wave can be polarised.
D The frequency of the wave is 1.0 Hz.

stemImage.alt: Question 14: The diagram shows the positions x of the particles along a progressive longitudinal wave at an 16 m s−. 1 instant in time. The wave travels at a speed of 10 30

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must read the wavelength from a particle-position diagram and recall basic wave properties.
questions.misconception: Taking compression-to-rarefaction distance as a full wavelength

explanation.body:
From the diagram, the wavelength is the distance from one compression to the next (or one rarefaction to the next): $\lambda = 16\ \mathrm{m}$.

$f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda} = \dfrac{16}{16} = 1.0\ \mathrm{Hz}$

perOption.A: 8.0 m is the distance from a compression to the next rarefaction, which is half a wavelength.
perOption.B: Particles at different positions along a progressive wave have different phases.
perOption.C: Only transverse waves can be polarised, and this wave is longitudinal.
perOption.D: Correct. $\lambda = 16\ \mathrm{m}$, so $f = v/\lambda = 1.0\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A transverse progressive wave travels along a rope.

The graph shows the variation of the displacement with time of a particle on the rope.

Taking displacement upwards as positive, at which point on the graph is the particle moving downwards with maximum speed?

[The sinusoidal displacement–time graph starts at zero and rises. A is the first downward zero crossing, B is the following trough, C is the next upward zero crossing, and D is the following crest.]

stemImage.alt: Question 13: A transverse progressive wave travels along a rope. The graph shows the variation of the displacement with time of a particle on the rope. Taking displacement u

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires finding the equilibrium crossings and reading the direction of motion there.
questions.misconception: Confusing maximum displacement with maximum speed

explanation.body: In simple harmonic motion, speed is greatest at equilibrium, so the candidates are A and C. Immediately after A the displacement is negative, so the particle is moving downwards there. Immediately after C it is positive, so the particle is moving upwards there.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: B is a turning point with zero instantaneous speed.
perOption.C: The particle crosses equilibrium at maximum speed but is moving upwards.
perOption.D: D is a turning point with zero instantaneous speed.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A point source emits $50.0\ \mathrm{W}$ of sound. A small microphone of area $0.85\ \mathrm{cm^2}$ detects the sound at $4.0\ \mathrm{m}$ from the source. What is the power detected by the microphone?

A $1.6\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{W}$
B $2.1\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{W}$
C $2.1\times10^{-1}\ \mathrm{W}$
D $2.5\times10^{-1}\ \mathrm{W}$

stemImage.alt: Question 17: A point source emits 50.0 W of sound. A small microphone of area 0.85 cm2 detects the sound at 4.0 m from the source. What is the power detected by the micropho

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must use spherical spreading and convert the microphone area to square metres.
questions.misconception: A square-centimetre conversion uses the linear conversion factor.

explanation.body: The microphone intercepts the fraction $a/(4\pi r^2)$ of the emitted power. Its detected power is $P'=\frac{0.85\times10^{-4}}{4\pi(4.0)^2}(50.0)=2.1\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the intercepted fraction for the stated area and radius.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Treating the numerical area in square centimetres as square metres makes the result $10^4$ times too large.
perOption.D: This is close to the intensity $50.0/(4\pi r^2)$, which still needs to be multiplied by the microphone area.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A narrow, parallel beam of unpolarised light is directed towards three ideal polarising filters. The beam meets the first filter with its axis of polarisation vertical. The axis of polarisation of the second filter is at an angle of $10^\circ$ to the first filter. The third filter has its axis of polarisation parallel to the second filter as shown.

[Unpolarised light passes through three filters labelled $0^\circ$, $10^\circ$ and $10^\circ$, in order. The outgoing beam is labelled transmitted light.]

The third filter is now turned.
At what angle must the third filter be with respect to the second filter so that the intensity of the transmitted light is reduced to $\frac13$ of the intensity of the unpolarised light?

A $34^\circ$
B $44^\circ$
C $47^\circ$
D $54^\circ$

stemImage.alt: Question 18: A narrow, parallel beam of unpolarised light is directed towards three ideal polarising filters. The beam meets the first filter with its axis of polarisation v

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must track the transmitted intensity and polarisation axis through three filters.
questions.misconception: Malus’ law always uses the angle relative to the first filter.

explanation.body: The first filter transmits $I/2$ from the unpolarised beam. By Malus’ law, the second transmits $(I/2)\cos^2 10^\circ$. For the third, $(I/2)\cos^2 10^\circ\cos^2\theta=I/3$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the second and third axes. Solving gives $\theta=34^\circ$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Adds the initial $10^\circ$ tilt and reports an angle relative to the first filter.
perOption.C: An angle of $47^\circ$ attenuates the beam below one-third of its initial intensity.
perOption.D: Using $54^\circ$ in the last Malus factor gives too little transmitted light.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: The graph shows how the displacement of particles in a longitudinal wave varies with the position $x$ along the wave. The wave travels towards the positive $x$ direction. Positive displacements are taken as displacements to the right of the equilibrium position. At the instant shown, which point along the wave has the maximum leftward velocity? [A sinusoidal graph of displacement against $x$ starts at zero and rises to crest A, falls through zero at B to trough C, then rises through zero at D to another crest before returning to zero.]

stemImage.alt: Question 12: The graph shows how the displacement of particles in a longitudinal wave varies with the position x along the wave. The wave travels towards the positive x dire

appearances.originalFile: TMJC/TMJC_2026_H2 Physics_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: It requires translating the spatial profile to infer the instantaneous direction and magnitude of particle velocity.
questions.misconception: Reading particle velocity directly from the spatial slope

explanation.body: Shift the displacement profile slightly to the right to represent a later instant. At D, the displacement then becomes negative, so the particle moves left. D is on the steepest rising part of the original profile, giving the greatest rate of decrease in displacement.

perOption.A: At the crest, the particle is at maximum displacement and is momentarily at rest.
perOption.B: The rightward shift of the profile increases the displacement at B, so the particle moves right.
perOption.C: At the trough, the particle is at its negative displacement extreme and is momentarily at rest.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The diagram shows the displacement of a transverse wave along a stretched cord at a particular instant. The wave travels from left to right with frequency 20 Hz.

What is the shortest time before the displacement at Q becomes zero?
questions.stemText: The diagram shows the displacement of a transverse wave along a stretched cord at a particular instant. The wave travels from left to right with frequency 20 Hz. What is the shortest time before the displacement at Q becomes zero? A 6.25 ms B 18.8 ms C 31.3 ms D 43.8 ms

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The student must use the direction of travel to identify which zero crossing will reach Q first.
questions.misconception: Using the nearest crossing on the wrong side of Q.

explanation.body: The period is $T=1/f=1/20\ \mathrm{s}=50\ \mathrm{ms}$. The wavelength spans eight divisions, and the right-moving zero crossing immediately to the left of Q is one division away. This is a phase difference of $\Delta\phi=2\pi/8=\pi/4$, so $\Delta t=(\Delta\phi/2\pi)T=6.25\ \mathrm{ms}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The first zero crossing reaches Q in one eighth of a period.
perOption.B: Uses the zero crossing three divisions to the right of Q, which moves away.
perOption.C: Uses the second zero crossing to arrive, five divisions to the left of Q.
perOption.D: Uses seven eighths of a period for a shift of only one division.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Two polarising filters, P and Q, are placed in front of a light sensor. Their transmission axes are initially parallel. Unpolarised light passes through them and the sensor records an intensity I.

Filter Q is then rotated while filter P remains fixed. Which angle through which Q may be rotated would reduce the detected intensity by 36%?
questions.stemText: Two polarising filters, P and Q, are placed in front of a light sensor. Their transmission axes are initially parallel. Unpolarised light passes through them and the sensor records an intensity I. Filter Q is then rotated while filter P remains fixed. Which angle through which Q may be rotated would reduce the detected intensity by 36%? A 23⁰ B 37⁰ C 50⁰ D 53⁰

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The calculation requires converting the percentage reduction to a transmitted fraction before applying Malus’ law.
questions.misconception: Using the percentage lost as the percentage transmitted.

explanation.body: By Malus’ law the detected intensity is $I_0\cos^2\theta$, where $I_0$ is the reading for parallel axes. A 36% reduction leaves $0.64I_0$, so $\cos^2\theta=0.64$. This gives $\theta=36.9^\circ$, or about $37^\circ$.

perOption.A: Transmits about 85% of the original reading, a drop of only about 15%.
perOption.B: Correct. About 64% of the original reading remains.
perOption.C: Transmits about 41% of the original reading, a drop of about 59%.
perOption.D: Treats the 36% lost as the fraction transmitted.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A plane polarized light wave of intensity $I_{0}$ is incident normally on a polarising filter. The initial intensity of the transmitted wave is 0. A second polarising filter is then inserted between the source and the first filter. Its transmission axis is at 40° to the transmission axis of the first filter, as shown.

What is the intensity of the transmitted wave from the filter combination?
questions.stemText: A plane polarized light wave of intensity I0 is incident normally on a polarising filter. The initial intensity of the transmitted wave is 0. A second polarising filter is then inserted between the source and the first filter. Its transmission axis is at 40° to the transmission axis of the first filter, as shown. What is the intensity of the transmitted wave from the filter combination? A 0 B 0.24 $I_{0}$ C 0.34 $I_{0}$ D 0.41 $I_{0}$

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires finding the incident angle at the inserted filter and applying Malus’ law twice.
questions.misconception: Using the angle between filters for both transmissions.

explanation.body: Zero initial transmission means the incident polarisation is perpendicular to the first filter's transmission axis. At the inserted second filter, $I_1=I_0\cos^2(90^\circ-40^\circ)=I_0\cos^2 50^\circ=0.413I_0$. At the original first filter, $I_2=I_1\cos^2 40^\circ=0.413I_0\times0.587=0.24I_0$.

perOption.A: Ignores the change in polarisation produced by the inserted filter.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses $40^\circ$ for both Malus’ law factors.
perOption.D: Stops at the intensity after the inserted filter.
